summary.text: 行 is drawn as a crossroads or thoroughfare. It is used for walking or going, and the road-like picture does not by itself tell us which spoken sense came first.

formation.text: A pictograph of a crossroads or thoroughfare as a whole. Although the Han-era Shuowen Jiezi analyzes 行 as 彳 plus 亍 and glosses it as human walking, the early graphic analysis does not establish those modern-looking parts as the original construction.

history.text: Oracle-bone forms are described as crossroads, with Western Zhou bronze forms continuing the shape; later records include Chu manuscripts, small seal script, and the Shuowen tradition. The curated image is a modern small-seal-style rendering, not an ancient artifact, and does not show the intervening graphic changes.
The Han-era Shuowen analysis divides 行 into 彳 and 亍 and explains it as walking. This is a historical lexicographic interpretation, not proof that the early graph was composed of those two parts.

uncertainties.text: The road-like picture supports a thoroughfare interpretation, but scholars differ on whether the spoken sense ‘road’ preceded ‘walk/go’; verbal uses are also reported in oracle-bone contexts. The graphic shape alone cannot settle the order.

A separate proposal says the graph was borrowed from a word for ‘place’ to write ‘go’ because of sound similarity. The dossier does not establish the source word’s chronology or a sound match, so this account remains unconfirmed.

senses.text: Verbal uses meaning movement are reported in oracle-bone inscriptions. These attest the use by that period but do not show that it was the earliest spoken sense.
The crossroads graph and cited oracle-bone contexts support a road-related use in this period; the interpretation of those contexts as ‘road’ is scholarly analysis.
德行 examples are reported in Warring States inscriptions and Chu slips, where 行 has a conduct-related use.
Later rhyme-book records distinguish a reading glossed ‘row/rank’ from readings associated with walking, order, and conduct; this evidence does not establish when the sense arose.

developments.text: A road-to-movement development has been proposed, but the reported early verbal uses and limits of graph-based chronology leave the direction unsettled.
A development from movement toward action or conduct has been proposed for later uses; the glosses and graph alone do not establish a complete sequence.

limitations.text: Reported reading categories and historical glosses do not by themselves provide a secure chronology connecting road, movement, row/rank, order, and conduct.

overview.text: 行 pictures a crossroads or thoroughfare. The character is used for walking or going, though the picture alone cannot tell us which spoken sense came first.
